sentences.text: The animal belongs to the genus Echinodon, which contains only one known species, Echinodon becklesii.
Its genus name translates to "prickly tooth," a reference to its unique dental structure.
Comparisons with related genera suggest the skull was approximately 62 mm long.
The premaxilla, or front part of the upper jaw, held only three teeth that lacked small serrations, distinguishing it from most early ornithischians.
The lower jaw, known as the dentary, contained eleven teeth, with the first two being specialized compared to other members of the group.
Research indicates the front tooth row was primarily used for cropping vegetation, based on wear patterns and jaw movement.
Sir Richard Owen formally described both the genus and the species Echinodon becklesii in 1861.
The initial finds consisted of jaw bones discovered by collector Samuel Beckles on a cliff at Durdlestone Bay on the Isle of Purbeck in southern England.
The specific name becklesii honors Samuel Beckles, the individual who found the fossil material.
Current studies accept an Early Cretaceous Berriasian age for Echinodon, making it the youngest and smallest known heterodontosaurid.
In 1971, Richard Thulborn placed Echinodon within the family Hypsilophodontidae, but Sereno was the first to reclassify it as a member of the family Heterodontosauridae.
This animal lived during the earliest Cretaceous, specifically the Berriasian epoch, roughly 145 to 140 million years ago in what is now southern England and possibly western France.
All known specimens have been recovered from the Purbeck Group of Dorset.
Sediment analysis suggests the Purbeck Group represented a lagoonal environment similar to the modern Mediterranean that became wetter over time.
Echinodon was originally considered a herbivorous lizard but was quickly revised to be an intermediate ornithischian.
The fossil was once referred to the clade Stegosauria based on dental anatomy and incorrectly attributed armor that was later identified as belonging to a turtle.
The age of the Purbeck Group containing Echinodon has been variably considered to be from the latest Jurassic or the earliest Cretaceous.
There is currently no evidence linking Echinodon to any specific bed in the Lulworth Formation of the Purbeck Group.
